title: Module: Plan
text: See how a supply chain fits together, then decide how much to buy, make and keep in stock. Every supply chain runs the same loop: plan, source, buy, receive, make, store, deliver and settle, then plan again. Goods move downstream from suppliers to customers, money moves upstream, and information (forecasts, orders, notices, invoices) moves both ways. Planning starts the loop: a forecast estimates what customers will buy, sales and operations planning (S&OP) agrees one plan across sales, operations and finance, and inventory policies such as the reorder point and safety stock decide when to replenish. A supply chain links suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and customers. Goods flow downstream, money upstream, information both ways. The loop: plan, source, buy, receive, make, store, deliver, settle, then plan again. Forecast → S&OP → inventory policy → planned orders. Reorder point = demand during lead time + safety stock; safety stock covers uncertainty. Three flows Goods go downstream, money goes upstream, information goes both ways. Forecasts are always wrong The aim is a forecast that is less wrong and a plan that copes with the error, using safety stock and short lead times. Reorder point Reorder when stock falls to demand during lead time plus safety stock.

title: Module: Source
text: Decide who to buy from and on what terms: spend analysis, RFI/RFQ/RFP, award, contract and supplier onboarding. Sourcing is the strategic start of buying, often called source-to-contract (S2C). Procurement analyses where money is spent, runs a sourcing event (an RFI, RFQ, RFP or auction), compares supplier offers on total cost rather than price alone, negotiates and awards. The result is a signed contract whose prices flow into catalogues and the ERP, and a supplier record set up correctly in master data. Source-to-contract plus procure-to-pay (modules 3, 4 and 8) make up source-to-pay (S2P). Source-to-contract: spend analysis → RFI/RFQ/RFP → evaluate and negotiate → award → contract → supplier onboarding. RFQ for a defined item and price; RFP for a proposed solution; RFI to learn who can supply. Compare suppliers on landed cost and reliability, not price alone. Contracts save money only when their prices reach catalogues and POs. S2P = S2C + P2P. S2P = S2C + P2P Source-to-contract picks the supplier and fixes the terms; procure-to-pay buys and pays against them. Total cost, not price Freight, duty, defects and late deliveries can make the cheapest quote the most expensive supplier. A contract only saves money if it is used Prices must reach catalogues and POs, or buyers keep paying the old price.

title: Module: Buy
text: Turn a need into an approved, legally binding purchase order, the start of procure-to-pay (P2P). Buying is where procure-to-pay (P2P) begins. Someone raises a purchase requisition (or planning creates one automatically). It is approved within delegated limits, then converted into a purchase order (PO), which is the company's commitment to the supplier. The supplier acknowledges it. Different needs use different instruments: standard POs, blanket or framework agreements with call-offs, scheduling agreements, consignment and service orders. P2P starts with a requisition: need → PR → approval → PO → acknowledgement. The PO is the external commitment; the PR is internal. An approval matrix routes requisitions by amount and category. Pick the instrument to the need: standard, blanket, scheduling agreement, consignment or service PO. EDI: 850 PO, 855 acknowledgement, 856 ASN, 810 invoice. The PO is the commitment A requisition is an internal request. The purchase order is what commits the company to the supplier. Approve by amount and category A delegation-of-authority matrix decides who approves which requisition. Services are different Services are bought on service POs and confirmed with a service entry sheet instead of a goods receipt.

title: Module: Receive
text: Expect, check and accept what arrives: the shipping notice, the goods receipt and quality inspection. Receiving proves the company got what it ordered. The supplier sends an advance shipping notice (ASN) so the warehouse can plan the dock. On arrival, staff scan pallet labels (GS1 SSCC), count and inspect, then post a goods receipt (GR) for what they accept. The receipt increases inventory and creates a liability on the GR/IR clearing account until the invoice arrives. Damaged goods go to blocked stock and back to the supplier; quality-critical items go through inspection first. ASN → dock → scan SSCC and count → inspect → goods receipt → putaway. Post only accepted quantity; return the rest to the supplier. A goods receipt adds stock and credits GR/IR until the invoice arrives. GS1: GTIN for products, SSCC for pallets and cartons, GLN for locations. Services are confirmed with a service entry sheet instead of a goods receipt. ASN first Knowing what is coming lets the warehouse plan labour and receive by scanning instead of counting. Receive what you accept Post only accepted quantity; the invoice will be matched against it. The receipt is a liability A goods receipt debits inventory and credits GR/IR until the supplier's invoice clears it.

title: Module: Make
text: Turn materials into finished products: bills of materials, MRP, production orders and what the product really cost. Manufacturing converts materials into products. A bill of materials (BOM) lists what goes into a product and a routing lists the operations. MRP takes demand, the BOM, stock and lead times and works out what to make or buy and when, creating planned orders. Production orders issue materials, record output and feed costing: inventory is valued at standard cost, moving average or FIFO, including landed costs such as freight and duty. Stock also moves between your own plants and companies, which has its own documents and tax. BOM = what goes in; routing = how it is made; MRP = what to make or buy, and when. MRP nets requirements against stock and open orders, then offsets by lead time. ERP owns the plan and cost; MES runs the floor. Inventory is valued at standard, moving average or FIFO cost, including landed cost. Transfers between GSTINs are taxable supplies, even inside one company. MRP explodes the BOM Demand for a finished product becomes dated requirements for every component, netted against stock. ERP plans, MES executes The ERP owns the plan and the cost; the manufacturing execution system runs the shop floor in real time. Landed cost Inventory cost = purchase price + freight + duty + insurance + handling.

title: Module: Store & fulfil
text: Hold stock accurately, then take, promise and pick customer orders across stores, websites and marketplaces. A warehouse management system (WMS) directs every movement in a warehouse: putaway, storage by bin, lot and expiry, cycle counts, and picking and packing. On the selling side, order-to-cash (O2C) begins: customers get a quote or order on a website, app, store, marketplace or by EDI. Pricing and credit are checked, and the order management system (OMS) promises only what is available (available-to-promise, ATP), reserves it and chooses which node fulfils it: a DC, a store (ship-from-store, BOPIS) or a supplier for drop-ship. Store: putaway → bin/lot tracking → cycle counts → pick → pack. FEFO for perishables; picking is the biggest warehouse labour cost. O2C starts here: quote → order → price and credit check → ATP → reserve → choose node. Sellable ATP = on hand − reserved − safety stock; credit exposure = open AR + open orders + new order. Omnichannel: one stock pool across DCs and stores (ship-from-store, BOPIS, BORIS). Location accuracy A WMS knows stock by bin and lot. If the bin is wrong, the picker cannot find it and the promise breaks. Promise you can keep Sellable ATP = on hand − reserved − safety stock. Every store is a warehouse Omnichannel retailers fulfil web orders from stores as well as DCs.

title: Module: Deliver
text: Move goods to the customer, across borders if needed, prove delivery and handle returns. A transportation management system (TMS) plans how goods move: it builds loads, chooses mode and carrier, tenders the shipment, tracks it and audits the freight bill. In India, most movements of goods worth over ₹50,000 need an e-way bill before the truck leaves. Across borders, global trade management handles classification, customs filings, duty and screening, and Incoterms decide who pays for and carries the risk of each leg. Delivery ends with a proof of delivery (POD), which often triggers the customer invoice; returns come back with a return authorisation (RMA). TMS: plan → tender → pick up → track → deliver → audit and pay the carrier. Consolidating loads is the main lever on freight cost. Incoterms split cost and risk; FOB and CIF are sea-only, FCA suits containers. Documents: bill of lading or air waybill, e-way bill, commercial invoice, certificate of origin, shipping bill or bill of entry, POD. Returns come back on an RMA; drop-ship lets the supplier deliver straight to your customer. Consolidate Combining small shipments into full loads is the biggest freight saving. Incoterms split cost and risk They decide where responsibility passes from seller to buyer, not who owns the goods. POD closes delivery Signed proof of delivery confirms the customer got the goods and often triggers billing.

title: Module: Settle
text: Close the money loop: match and pay supplier invoices (end of P2P), bill and collect from customers (end of O2C), and report tax. Settling turns the physical flow into money. On the buy side, accounts payable captures the supplier invoice, matches it against the PO and goods receipt (three-way match) and pays it in a payment run, which ends procure-to-pay. On the sell side, billing issues the customer invoice, accounts receivable applies incoming payments and chases late ones, which ends order-to-cash. Tax rides on every invoice: in India, CGST and SGST within a state, IGST between states, e-invoices with an IRN and input tax credit. How fast cash goes out and comes in decides the cash conversion cycle. Pay: invoice → three-way match → payment run → remittance; GR/IR should clear. Collect: customer invoice → cash application → collections; apply what was paid and track deductions. DSO = receivables ÷ revenue × days; CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO. GST: CGST + SGST within a state, IGST between states; e-invoices get an IRN. Pay MSME (micro and small) suppliers within 45 days in India. Three-way match Pay only what was ordered (PO), received (GRN) and billed (invoice), within tolerance. Cash is the finish line O2C ends when the customer's payment is applied to the invoice, not when the parcel is delivered. Place of supply Supplier location and place of supply decide CGST + SGST (same state) or IGST (different states).

text: How organisations decide what to buy, from whom, at what price and on what terms, and how they keep suppliers performing. title: Logistics & Transportation
text: Moving goods between nodes: choosing modes and carriers, agreeing who pays and who carries the risk, and the documents that travel with the freight. Modes of transport Each mode trades cost, speed, capacity and reliability. Freight and carrier management Buying, planning and controlling freight so goods move reliably at the right cost. Incoterms and shipping documentation Incoterms 2020 are the ICC rules that define where risk passes from seller to buyer, and who pays for carriage, insurance and customs. Top 20 logistics terms

title: Inventory Management
text: Holding the right stock in the right place: classifying it, costing it, measuring it and replenishing it. Types of inventory Inventory is classified by its stage and its purpose. ABC analysis Rank items by annual consumption value. A few A items carry most of the value and deserve tight control; many C items need only simple rules. Inventory costs, formulas and KPIs Inventory costs money to buy, to order and to hold, and it costs sales when you run out. Top 20 inventory terms

title: Distribution, Fulfillment & Warehousing
text: Getting orders out of the building and to the customer: who runs the warehouse, how it is laid out and automated, and what good looks like. 1PL to 5PL How much of logistics you outsource, and to whom. Distribution and fulfillment automation Automation removes walking, lifting and sorting, the biggest costs in a DC. Best practices for distribution centers What well-run DCs do consistently. Warehouse design and layout Layout decides travel distance, congestion and capacity.

title: Demand Planning & Forecasting
text: Estimating demand, measuring how wrong the estimate was, and agreeing one plan across the business. Forecasting methods Qualitative methods use judgement; quantitative methods use data. Most companies combine both. Forecast accuracy (MAPE, MAD) Measure error to improve the forecast and to size safety stock. Sales and operations planning (S&OP) A monthly cycle that agrees one plan across sales, operations and finance.

title: Supply Chain Strategy & Design
text: Structural choices made once and lived with for years: how centralised to be, what to make or buy, when to customise, and which operating model fits the product. Centralized vs decentralized supply chains Who decides, and where inventory and operations sit. Make vs buy decisions Produce in-house, or outsource? Compare cost, capability, control, capacity and strategic importance. Postponement and agile strategies Delay the final configuration until demand is clearer, so one generic stock serves many variants. 12 supply chain models

title: Risk Management & Resilience
text: Identifying what could break the chain, reducing the chance and the damage, and recovering fast when it happens. Supply chain risk management and mitigation Identify → assess (likelihood × impact) → mitigate → monitor. Business continuity planning A plan to keep critical operations running during and after a disruption. ISO 22301 is the common standard. Cybersecurity in supply chain Attackers reach companies through their suppliers, software and logistics partners. Major supply chain disruptions

title: Continuous Improvement: Lean, Kaizen, Six Sigma
text: Methods for removing waste and variation, step by step, with the people who do the work. Lean principles and the 8 wastes Lean maximises customer value while removing waste. Five principles: define value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, pursue perfection. Kaizen "Change for the better": continuous, small improvements by everyone, every day, plus focused kaizen events of a few days on one process. Lean Six Sigma Six Sigma reduces variation using data; lean removes waste. Together they improve speed and quality. Continuous improvement tools

title: Technology in Supply Chain
text: The systems that run supply chains today and the technologies changing them. ERP systems (SAP, Oracle and others) ERP is the system of record for finance, purchasing, inventory and sales. Specialist systems (S2P, OMS, WMS, TMS, planning) connect around it. AI agents innovating supply chain Software agents that watch data, explain exceptions, recommend actions and, within limits you set, act: re-routing an order, releasing a held invoice, raising a purchase order. Intelligent document processing (IDP) Supply chains run on documents: invoices, order confirmations, bills of lading, packing lists, certificates of analysis, customs entries, delivery receipts and contracts. IDP reads them into validated data with OCR, classification, extraction, confidence scoring, business rules and human review; GenAI adds template-free extraction, summaries and Q&A. Autonomous supply chain Planning and execution that sense, decide and act with little human intervention. Most companies move through levels: manual → assisted → partly automated → highly automated → autonomous for routine decisions, with people managing exceptions and policy. Emerging technologies

title: Sustainability & ESG
text: Measuring and reducing environmental impact, keeping materials in use, and making sure products are made responsibly. Carbon footprint measurement Companies report greenhouse gas emissions in three scopes, using the GHG Protocol. Circular supply chains Keep products and materials in use for as long as possible instead of take-make-dispose. Ethical sourcing Making sure suppliers respect human rights, labour standards and the environment.

title: Supply Chain Analytics
text: Turning supply chain data into decisions: what happened, why, what will happen, and what to do. Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive Four levels, each answering a harder question. SCM control tower A central hub that combines data from ERP, OMS, WMS, TMS and partners to give end-to-end visibility, raise alerts, support decisions and coordinate responses. Transparency and visibility Visibility is knowing where your goods, orders and inventory are right now. Transparency is sharing how and where products are made with customers, investors and regulators. Supply chain KPI tree

title: Supply chain digital twin dashboard
text: Replay a day of goods, information and money moving through a network. Learners and stakeholders struggle to see how POs, receipts, orders, shipments and payments relate. A visual replay of linked events makes the three flows concrete and doubles as a demo shell for later projects.

title: Synthetic supply chain data generator
text: Linked, realistic test data with deliberate errors, reused by every other project. Every project needs believable data: suppliers with GSTINs, POs that partially deliver, invoices with errors, orders with returns. Hand-made fixtures are small and too clean.

title: Mini sourcing platform with live reverse auction
text: RFI/RFQ/RFP events, supplier portal, weighted scoring, award to contract. Sourcing teams compare quotations in spreadsheets, lose bid history and cannot show why a supplier won. Awards often never reach the price records used on POs.

title: Supplier onboarding and risk service
text: Onboarding forms, tax-ID checks, dual-approved bank changes, risk score. Payment fraud often starts with a fake bank-change request. Supplier onboarding is slow, unvalidated and spread across email.

title: Procure-to-pay core platform
text: Requisition → approval → PO → EDI → goods receipt → GR/IR accounting. The backbone every other buy-side project plugs into. It must handle versioned POs, configurable approvals and correct accounting entries.

title: 2/3/4-way matching engine
text: A pure, fully tested matching library with event-driven re-matching. Matching rules are often buried in AP code and impossible to test. Held invoices wait for manual re-matching even after the missing receipt arrives.

title: AP automation platform
text: Capture → extraction → validation → matching → review → posting, end to end. Invoice-rag answers questions about invoices; real AP needs those invoices validated, matched to POs and receipts, reviewed by people when unsure, and posted to the ledger.

title: Invoice extraction evaluation harness
text: Measure field accuracy per supplier layout and compare extraction engines. Teams change OCR models, prompts or chunking without knowing whether accuracy went up or down for the suppliers that matter.

title: GST e-invoice validator and reconciler
text: Validate e-invoice JSON, verify signed QR data, reconcile against purchase records. Indian businesses receive e-invoices with an IRN and signed QR code. AP must confirm the invoice is genuine and matches purchase records before claiming input tax.

title: Store fulfilment app (BOPIS and ship-from-store)
text: Store associates pick, handle shorts, and hand over orders; capacity-aware routing. Stores fulfilling online orders need a fast picking flow, a clear process when the shelf is empty, and protection from overload during peak.

title: "Available near you" search read model
text: Product search with live per-store availability and a freshness SLO. Shoppers want to know if a product is in stock nearby right now. Search indexes lag behind inventory and show stale availability.

title: Order orchestration and holds
text: Order state machine, partial cancels, fraud/payment holds, ship-to-store fallback. omni-retail reserves and routes; real orders also pause for fraud checks, wait for payment, get partially cancelled and need a fallback when a pickup store is short.

title: Optimal order sourcing solver
text: Integer programming for multi-SKU, multi-node baskets vs greedy heuristics. Greedy split routing is fast but can create extra parcels and cost. An optimiser finds the true minimum-cost plan; the question is whether it is fast enough at checkout.

title: Mini WMS
text: Locations, LPNs, ASN receiving, putaway, replenishment, waves vs streaming, scanner UI. The warehouse is where inventory accuracy is won or lost. Building a WMS teaches location-level inventory, task-driven work and the OMS/ERP contracts around it.

title: Warehouse simulation: waves vs order streaming
text: Discrete-event simulation of pickers and robots on a grid. Choosing between fixed waves and continuous release is usually argued, not measured. A simulation makes the trade-off visible.

title: CPQ-lite: configure, price, quote
text: Quote revisions, price lists, discount authority, PDF quotes, quote-to-order. Sales teams send quotes from spreadsheets, approve discounts by chat, and re-key accepted quotes into the order system.

title: Cash application engine
text: Parse bank statements and remittances; auto-match payments; create deductions. Payments arrive with poor references. AR teams match them by hand, and short payments silently become write-offs.

title: Inventory accuracy and cycle counting service
text: ABC-based counts, variance approvals, shrinkage analytics by store. Store inventory drifts through theft, damage and missed scans, which breaks online promises. Counting everything is too expensive, so counts must be targeted.

title: DC-to-store transfer orders and in-transit ATP
text: Stores replenished from DCs; in-transit stock counted in availability. In omni-retail every node buys from suppliers. Real retailers replenish stores from DCs, and stock on a truck should be promisable for future dates.

title: Carrier aggregator and tracking hub
text: One API over many carriers: rates, labels, normalised tracking events. Every carrier has a different API, label format and status vocabulary. Customer service needs one consistent tracking view.

title: Last-mile route planner for Bengaluru
text: Vehicle routing with time windows on real road networks. Same-day delivery needs routes that respect time windows, vehicle capacity and traffic, recalculated as orders arrive.

title: Demand forecasting service driving reorder points
text: Forecasts by SKU × location with versioned plans that update safety stock and ROP. Static reorder points ignore seasonality and promotions. Forecast-driven parameters reduce stockouts and excess, if the plan reliably reaches execution.

title: S&OP plan comparison tool
text: Compare demand, supply and financial plan versions with variance waterfalls. Monthly S&OP meetings argue over which spreadsheet is current. Versioned plans with clear variances focus the discussion.

title: Returns disposition engine
text: Decide restock, refurbish, return-to-vendor or liquidate; raise RTV debit notes. Returned items lose value every day they wait. Disposition decisions are inconsistent and supplier credits for defective goods are often never claimed.

title: Supply chain copilot (tool-using agent)
text: Ask "why is order 101233 late?" and get an answer grounded in your services. Answering operational questions means checking OMS, WMS, carrier and P2P screens. An agent that calls those APIs read-only can answer in seconds, if it is safe and auditable.

title: Streaming anomaly detection on supply chain events
text: Flag unusual PO prices, invoice amounts and inventory adjustments in real time. Fraud and errors hide in volume: a price 30% above contract, a midnight inventory adjustment, an invoice just under an approval limit.

title: Reference architecture: the connected platform
text: Run P2P, OMS, WMS and AP together on any Kubernetes with GitOps and full observability. Individual services prove skills; a running, observable platform proves architecture. This is the capstone that ties every project together.

title: Integration layer with replayable dead letters
text: Mapping, routing, retries, DLQ and a replay UI between your services and mock ERPs. Integrations fail at 2 a.m. and someone replays messages by hand. A good integration layer makes failures visible, explainable and safely replayable.

title: ERP adapter kit (anti-corruption layer)
text: One canonical P2P/O2C model with pluggable adapters that mimic SAP, Oracle and Coupa styles. Real landscapes connect to different ERPs and procurement suites. Coding directly to one vendor's objects spreads its vocabulary everywhere. An anti-corruption layer keeps your core vendor-neutral.

title: Execution and planning contract test suite
text: AsyncAPI + Pact contracts for OMS → WMS release and planning → ERP recommendations. OMS, WMS and planning tools from different vendors meet at message contracts. Most integration incidents are contract drift nobody noticed.

title: SAP S/4HANA Materials Management and adjacent products
text: SAP S/4HANA is an ERP. Materials Management (MM) is its purchasing and inventory heart: requisitions, POs, goods receipts and invoice verification. Around it sit SAP Ariba (source-to-pay on the business network), SAP EWM (warehouse), SAP TM (transport) and SAP IBP (planning).

title: Coupa business spend management
text: Coupa is a cloud source-to-pay and spend-management suite. It is strongest where many employees buy things and many suppliers send invoices: requisitioning, catalogs, approvals, supplier collaboration, invoicing and spend visibility. It usually runs alongside an ERP that keeps the general ledger and often pays suppliers.

title: Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP and SCM
text: Oracle Fusion Cloud covers ERP (Financials, Payables), Procurement (Purchasing, Self Service Procurement, Sourcing, Supplier Portal) and SCM (Order Management, Inventory, Warehouse Management, Transportation Management, Supply Chain Planning). One vendor can cover most of the commercial lifecycle.

title: Manhattan Active platform: Omni, Warehouse Management, Transportation Management
text: Manhattan focuses on supply chain execution and omnichannel commerce. Manhattan Active Omni handles order management, store fulfilment and customer service; Manhattan Active Warehouse Management runs DCs with order streaming and built-in WES; Manhattan Active Transportation Management covers freight. It sits next to an ERP, not in place of one.

title: Blue Yonder Cognitive Solutions for planning and execution
text: Blue Yonder (formerly JDA Software, part of Panasonic) spans supply chain planning (demand, supply, S&OP, category and space planning) and execution (warehouse, transportation, order management, returns), now positioned as Cognitive Solutions on the Blue Yonder Platform. Many retailers know it first for demand forecasting and replenishment.

title: Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance and Supply Chain Management
text: Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance and Supply Chain Management cover procurement, inventory, warehouse management, production, planning and finance in one ERP, with Commerce for retail and Intelligent Order Management for orchestration. It integrates with the Microsoft Power Platform and Dataverse.

title: IBM Sterling Order Management and B2B Integration
text: IBM Sterling Order Management is a distributed order management system used by large retailers and manufacturers for global inventory visibility, sourcing and orchestration. IBM Sterling B2B Integrator and Supply Chain Business Network handle EDI and partner integration.

title: Kinaxis Maestro concurrent planning
text: Kinaxis Maestro (formerly RapidResponse) is a supply chain planning platform known for concurrent planning: one data model for demand, supply, inventory and capacity, with fast what-if scenarios.

title: o9 Solutions planning platform
text: o9 Solutions provides a planning platform for demand planning, supply planning, integrated business planning and revenue management, built on an Enterprise Knowledge Graph that models the business.
